name: Esther Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Esther, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at the lithium pit, the rig that drills the rows of holes the blasters fill, and I lead the drill crew on days. This year I'm also the operator they picked for the trial of an autonomous drill, so half my shift I'm driving my own rig and half I'm watching the self-drilling one and writing up what it gets wrong. I love that part, honestly, it's like teaching an apprentice who never gets tired. What wears me out is the pay, because we're on a contractor rate that's well under what the big companies pay.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Daniel, my partner, stays home with our two, six and ten, and does some delivery driving in the evenings. We've got a mortgage on a newish house on the estate they built for the mine, and money's tight, I'd say three weeks from trouble at any point. There's nowhere else to work around here except the mine and the shops that serve it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use an AI assistant every day, for the drill logs, for planning our budget, even to help my ten-year-old with her reading. I'm the one people at work come to when the tablet does something weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and leave it there. People who were scared can relax, and people who were selling it can calm down. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit let down. I like the trial and I thought it might lead somewhere for me. But I'd still be the drill lead with good tools, which isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the AI for my logs and planning, keep improving the drill trial even if it's small. I'd ask the company for a pay step for the trial work, because that's real extra work. And keep chipping at the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the idea, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay step. How would you make that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the numbers. I've logged every fault on the autonomous rig for nine months, and my notes fixed the hole-depth problem. I'd put that on one page and ask for what it's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time the AI saves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more drill data, if I'm honest, I like it. But Daniel would want me home earlier. So maybe an hour more with the kids, which is the right answer.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool and leave it there, telling both the worried and the sellers to relax. That's about as political as I get.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a bit let down, because I enjoy the autonomous drill trial and hoped it would lead somewhere. Still, being drill lead with good tools isn't bad.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for logs and planning and keeps refining the drill trial. Asks for a pay step for the trial work using her fault records, and keeps paying down the car loan.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored by the idea.
S0.quote: I've logged every fault on the autonomous rig for nine months, and my notes fixed the hole-depth problem.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is already inside the automation story at her mine, so a plateau feels like a missed chance rather than relief. She argues for pay with data, not politics. Even the extra free time she'd half spend on drill data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to happen either way, so workers should get in early and help shape it. I'd tell the crew that the people who understand the machines will run them. I'd probably post some of what I've learned from the trial, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me, if I play it right. I already know the autonomous drill better than anyone on site. The risk is the money, because if there's a gap between my old job ending and the new one starting, we've got three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the autonomous drill rollout formally, with a job title and pay. I'd sign up for the online certificate in mine automation, nights, with the AI helping me study. And I'd start a small side thing doing drone surveys for the farms around us, because I've already got the licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a bit of excitement. The money keeps me from being cocky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the drone licence. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago I got curious and did it online, then bought a second-hand drone with my tax refund. I've done three jobs for farmers checking fences and dams. It's small money, but it's money that isn't the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raúl, my offsider, he's a good driller but he hates tablets. I've been trying to show him the autonomous rig and he walks off. I'd keep at him, because I don't want to be the one who trained the machine that took his job.

S1.say: I'd say change will come either way, so workers should get in early and help shape it. I'd tell the crew those who understand the machines will run them, and might post lessons from the trial.
S1.think: Honestly I think it's good for me if I play it right, since I know the autonomous drill best on site. The risk is a gap between jobs when we only have three weeks of money.
S1.do: Asks to lead the autonomous drill rollout formally with a title and pay. Takes an online mine automation certificate at night with AI help, and grows a side business doing drone surveys for nearby farms.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a little excited, kept humble by money worries.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the one who trained the machine that took his job.
S1.fieldNote: Esther sees steady change as an opening and already has a side income started. Her one real worry is a short gap between jobs, given thin savings. Her concern for her offsider shows she knows her success could cost others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone, and the government should cushion people and make companies give notice. I'm not normally for big government stuff, but that's just common sense when it's this quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even my place in the rollout only lasts a year or so, because the AI learns to supervise itself. I'd ride that year for all it's worth. Then I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the company in month one and offer to lead the rollout across all their sites, travelling if needed, for the best rate I can get. Everything extra goes into savings. I'd push the drone work, and use the AI every night to look at what work is still left for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one with a plan, and here my plan has a short fuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you feel any guilt helping roll it out faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, some. But if I don't, someone from the city does, and they don't know our crews. At least I'd make sure the safety side was done right and that people got told straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if you're travelling between sites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel holds the fort, which he already does. The kids would hate me being away, especially the six-year-old. I'd tell them it's a year, and I'd mean it, but I'd be guessing.

S2.say: I'd say two years is too fast, and the government should cushion people and make companies give notice. I'm not usually for big government, but this is common sense.
S2.think: I think even my role in the rollout lasts only about a year before AI supervises itself. I'd ride that year as hard as I could, and after that I don't know.
S2.do: Offers in month one to lead the rollout across all the company's sites, travelling for the best rate, and saves every extra dollar. Pushes the drone work and uses AI nightly to search for work still done by people.
S2.feel: Anxious, because her plan now has a short fuse.
S2.quote: I'm usually the one with a plan, and here my plan has a short fuse.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fast picture doesn't break Esther, but it shortens her horizon to one year. She accepts some guilt about speeding the rollout, reasoning that a local is better than an outsider. Her centrist views bend towards government support when speed is extreme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, and the people who start now will be fine. I'd say companies should train their own people first rather than hiring outsiders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get three or four years leading automation at the mine, and that's real money compared with now. The question is what comes after, and I'd want the drone business big enough to stand on by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the automation job title in year one, and finish the certificate by year two. I'd put every spare dollar into savings first, then into a better drone and some survey software, maybe two thousand by year three. Daniel might help with the bookings, since he's good with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the drone business. Wouldn't AI and robots do that too, by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. You've got me there. Maybe the business becomes looking after a fleet of drones for farmers who don't want to deal with them, I honestly don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's fine to like machines, I do, but learn to deal with people too. My ten-year-old wants to be a vet. I'd tell her that's a great idea.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but workable and those who start now will be fine. Companies should train their own people first rather than hire outsiders.
S3.think: I think I'd get three or four years leading automation at the mine, which is better money than now. After that I'd want the drone business big enough to stand on.
S3.do: Gets the automation job title in year one and finishes the certificate by year two. Builds savings first, then puts about two thousand into a better drone and survey software by year three, with Daniel handling bookings.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more interested than scared.
S3.quote: Probably, yes. You've got me there.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Esther's confidence returns and she lays out a clear sequence. When pressed on whether her drone plan would also be automated, she conceded the point openly. She wants her daughters to build people skills as well as tech skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and I'd be telling everyone on the crew to start something now, not in year eight. I'd offer to teach anyone who wants it on the tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years suits me well. I'd have a good stretch leading automation, a real side business, and the kids would be older. By fifty-three I'd hope to be working for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the certificate, take the automation role, and grow the drone survey work steadily, maybe hire someone part-time by year six. We'd save three months of bills by year four, which would be a first for us. And I'd run Saturday tablet sessions for the crew at the community hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that you'd find hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching the people who don't move. Ten years gives everyone a chance and some won't take it, like Raúl. I'd find that harder than the two-year one in a way, because there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be a miner, in your own head, by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd be the miner who flies drones and argues with software. You don't stop being a miner just because you're not underground or in the cab.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and urge the crew to start something now, not in year eight. I'd offer to teach anyone who wanted it on the tablets.
S4.think: I think ten years suits me: a good stretch leading automation, a real side business and older kids. By fifty-three I'd hope to be working for myself.
S4.do: Completes the certificate, takes the automation role and grows the drone survey business, perhaps hiring part-time help by year six. Builds three months of savings by year four and runs Saturday tablet sessions for the crew.
S4.quote: You don't stop being a miner just because you're not underground or in the cab.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits Esther's adaptability, and she sounds genuinely calm. Her hardest feeling is about colleagues who won't use the time. She keeps her miner identity even while picturing a very different job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my plans need a few years of runway and we don't have savings to cover a gap. What would help is a short bridge payment between jobs during a changeover, and companies having to train and hire locals for the new roles first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want any of this. I'm not sure the answer's yes for everyone. I like it, but I'm not most people.

headlineQuote: It's like teaching an apprentice who never gets tired.
portrait: Esther Silva is a 43-year-old blast-hole drill lead at a lithium pit on a contractor rate, with a partner who stays home and drives deliveries, two young children, a mortgage and about three weeks of money in hand. She uses AI every day, leads the trial of an autonomous drill and runs a small drone survey side business. She stays calm through the plateau and steady change, seeing a role leading automation, and turns anxious only when two years leaves her plan with a short fuse. With five or ten years she plans to build the drone work into her own business, while worrying about crew mates who won't move.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her plans need a few years of runway and the family has no savings to cover a gap.
whatWouldHelp: A short bridge payment between jobs during a changeover, and rules requiring companies to train and hire locals for new roles first.
